title: The true mint
hookLine: let self-control be the furnace, patience the goldsmith, understanding the anvil (Japji 38)
tomorrow: the Japji ends with air, water and earth. which one is the guru?
last: SMALL KINDNESSES · TO KNOW ONE ANOTHER · NO COMPULSION.

cards: A barista weighing beans, a cashier counting change: some work is mostly counting. The janamsakhis say Guru Nanak had a job like that. In Sultanpur, he kept the governor's stores, weighing out grain.
One day, they say, he was counting the measures aloud, one, two, three, and at thirteen, tera, he went no further. Tera also means yours. And he kept on weighing and saying it: tera, tera.

teach.b: Keep that picture of a man at a scale, because the Japji's thirty-eighth stanza is a workshop.
Let self-control be the furnace, it says, and patience the goldsmith. Let understanding be the anvil, and knowledge the hammer. Let the fear of God be the bellows, and discipline the fire.
Let love be the crucible, and melt the nectar in it. In that true mint, the Word is coined. And the stanza ends: this is the work of those on whom His gracious glance falls.

teach.h: STAMPED WITH THE WORD, UNDER GRACE.
teach.b: So, in the Japji, a life is shaped like a coin, slowly, by discipline and love, and stamped with the Shabad, the Word.
Both halves are there: the patient work at the anvil, and nadar, the glance of grace, without which none of it happens.
And the detail to keep: in the Japji's workshop, the goldsmith isn't skill or speed. It's patience.

how: Sikhs recite the Japji each morning; its thirty-eighth stanza, the true mint, is taught as the shaping of character by discipline, love and the Guru's Word, under God's grace.

o: an honest price paid at a market stall
a place where coins are made for temple offerings
a life shaped slowly and stamped with the Word

s: in Japji 38, patience is the goldsmith
self-control the furnace, patience the goldsmith, understanding the anvil.
the Japji says a life is shaped by effort alone
the stanza ends on the gracious glance: this is the work of those on whom it falls.
the story says Nanak stopped at thirteen because he lost count
tera means thirteen and yours; he kept weighing and saying yours.

games.q: a friend asks: if grace does it, why practice? and if practice does it, why grace? how does Japji 38 hold both?
o: the mint needs furnace, anvil and goldsmith, and the stanza ends on grace's glance: both.
only grace counts; the tools in the stanza are just decoration.
only effort counts; the glance at the end is a figure of speech.
games.why: Japji 38 lists the disciplines that shape the coin, then says this is the work of those on whom His glance of grace falls.

practice: Find a coin, or something small and metal, and hold it in your palm. Look at what was stamped into it, and feel its weight. Then name, to yourself, one habit you're shaping slowly, and the next small strike you could give it.
